main_html:
Fresno–Clovis, California · clinic-published fee evidence · reviewed October 29, 2026

Fresno I-693 medical exam cost: one clinic's published $750 base fee, and how to turn it into a written total.

What the advertised $750 covers: what should you know?

AFC Urgent Care Fresno advertises a $750 base immigration medical examination for adults and children. The clinic publishes additional testing and vaccine charges separately. Treat the amount as one clinic's advertised examination fee, not the total for every applicant, a market average, or a guaranteed quote. The practical consequence is that two applicants quoted the same $750 can pay very different final amounts: the examination fee is the only part of the price that is the same for everyone, and it is often the smaller part of the bill for an applicant who needs several vaccines or a chest X-ray.

Itemized tests and vaccines: what should you know?

The Fresno clinic lists RPR syphilis testing at $46, gonorrhea testing at $90, QuantiFERON tuberculosis testing at $100, and an indicated chest X-ray at $90. Published vaccine prices include Tdap $65, MMR $110 and seasonal influenza $45. Which tests or vaccines are needed depends on the applicant and current clinical and immigration requirements; simply adding everything would mislead readers. Ask the clinic to mark each published line as required for you, possible depending on results, or not applicable, and to tell you which of those decisions can only be made after the first visit. A line that cannot be resolved until results return is not a hidden fee, but it is a number you should know might appear.

Turning an advertised fee into a comparable written quote: what should you know?

Advertised fees are only comparable when they describe the same scope. Before you book, ask each office to put the following in writing, in this order, so two quotes can be set side by side:

  1. The base examination fee, and whether it differs by applicant age.
  2. Each laboratory test the clinic expects you to need, priced individually, and whether the price includes the laboratory's own charge or only the collection.
  3. Each vaccine or titer, priced individually, with a note on whether a titer showing existing immunity removes the vaccine charge.
  4. Whether an indicated chest X-ray is performed on site at the published price or referred out and billed separately by the imaging provider.
  5. The cost of the follow-up visit, and whether it is included in the base fee or billed again.
  6. Any charge for completing, signing, sealing, or copying the paperwork.
  7. What happens to the money already paid if the examination cannot be completed.

A quote that answers all seven is comparable to another quote that answers all seven. A quote that answers only the first is a starting price.

How many visits are needed?

The practice describes at least two visits for the immigration medical examination. The follow-up commonly occurs after laboratory results have returned. Confirm the appointment timetable with the office before travel, because processing time and available appointments can change. Ask specifically what happens if a result is abnormal or indeterminate: an additional test, a referral, or a treatment course can add both visits and cost, and it is better to know the clinic's usual path before you are standing in it.

Records to gather before the first visit: what should you know?

The single most effective way to hold your own cost down is to arrive with documentation of what you have already had, because a documented vaccine does not need to be repeated and a documented immunity may remove a charge. Before the first appointment, assemble a valid identity document; any immunization record you hold, including records from another country, with dates; results of any recent tuberculosis testing or chest imaging; a current list of medications; and records relating to any condition the clinician will need to assess. Bring originals or clear copies rather than a verbal history. If a record is in another language, ask the office in advance whether a translation is required and who may provide it.

Documents and questions: what should you know?

Bring a valid identity document, available immunization records and relevant medical records, and follow the latest USCIS Form I-693 instructions. Ask for an itemized written estimate that distinguishes the exam, laboratory tests, vaccines or titers, X-rays, follow-up visits and copies. Ask when the required completed paperwork will be delivered and whether extra charges apply.

Timing, payment and paperwork delivery: what should you know?

Cost and timing are the same question when a filing deadline is involved, because an examination that has to be repeated is an examination paid for twice. Ask how long after the follow-up visit the completed paperwork is normally ready, whether it is handed to you sealed or sent, and what the office does if a result is delayed. Ask when payment is due relative to each visit, which payment methods are accepted, and whether any part is refundable if the examination cannot be completed. Finally, ask how you obtain an additional copy later and what that costs — the one charge applicants most often meet after they thought the matter was closed.

How do you know a quote is still incomplete?

A quote is still incomplete when it gives one number without naming the examination scope it covers; when it prices tests as a bundle without saying which are required for you; when it leaves the follow-up visit unpriced; when it is silent on paperwork, sealing and copies; when the signing clinician is unnamed; or when nobody will say what happens to the payment if the examination cannot be completed. Any one of those is worth a second call before you book, and none of them is an unreasonable thing to ask.

Editorial independence: what should you know?

This guide is independent information, not medical or immigration legal advice. No clinic mentioned is verified as an advertiser, contracted referral recipient or guaranteed appointment provider. Fees, clinic policies, designation and vaccination guidance can change. Confirm directly with the clinic and the appropriate official government service.
